# Javelin Robotics announces truck reservations program


[Addwiteey Chrungoo](https://medium.com/@achrungoo?source=post_page---byline--7199c3671e8c---------------------------------------)


4 min read


·


Jun 23, 2023


--


In my last post, I shared the story of[Blackbird: Our first highly automated truck](https://medium.com/javelin-robotics/the-story-of-blackbird-javelins-first-highly-automated-truck-197659e1b4f0) . Today, I’m thrilled to unveil yet another milestone towards commercializing our tag-team approach to autonomous trucking.


Over the last 2 years, Javelin discretely launched an invite-only Partner Reservations Program. I’m proud to (finally) announce that more than **two dozen fleets** joined this invite-only program and became the first ever batch of mid-market trucking carriers to sign agreements and collectively reserve the first **1600 Javelin-equipped trucks** .


> “More than two dozen fleets joined this invite-only program and collectively reserved more than 1600 Javelin-equipped trucks”


These agreements are first of its kind in our industry — both in terms of the type of autonomy, how its expected to be used, as well as the type of fleet customers it serves.


### **The mid-market customer**


North America has more than a million carriers. Out of these, there are close to 4K carriers that own or operate between 100 to 2000 trucks. Like mega-carriers, mid-market fleets are sophisticated enough, but differ in terms of their size, scale, and operational characteristics.


These fleets essentially haul tonnes of freight across the United States and Canada, but do it ever so differently — operations are not always consistent back and forth movements on specific lanes. Fleets need to reroute vehicles to different locations, have flexibility and quickly adapt to changing demand in pursuit of optimization.


> This variability makes it impractical for several mid-market trucking businesses to adopt unmanned trucks, especially via the commonly proposed transfer hub model. Finding, hiring and maintaining a local pool of drivers near every city you have to pick up from and or deliver to and maintaining an effective distribution of such local drivers, is challenging even for reasonably sized boutique businesses.


These characteristics make mid-market fleets the ideal first partners for Javelin. Our approach affords flexibility and enables capacity and efficiency gains without disrupting a trucking company’s current operating processes.


> “We always remind ourselves that we are NOT solving a self-driving problem for our partners. We at Javelin are solving ‘ **asset utilization** ’ and ‘capacity shortage’ problems in their businesses”


### **How we are working together**


We believe its important for Javelin to be focussed on technology, but wearing the shoes of your customer often results in deep insights which are invaluable. You not only generate industry credibility, but also remove several operational blockers for developing autonomous driving.


Over the last two years, we’ve embedded ourselves deep into customer operations, hauling hundreds of loads for them (we’ll share more on this later) while testing. We share information on routes, where and how to launch, which states to target, which conditions to generalize for and so on and getting that feedback loop going helps us learn faster.


The way our agreements are setup, **fleets will order trucks of their choice and Javelin will equip those trucks with its highly automated driving system, that includes hardware and software** . The trucks will be owned and operated by fleets, have a human driver onboard, and Javelin will offer its technology as a per-mile software subscription for all miles driven by an asset. We’ll share more about our subscription model and its economics soon.


### **Second driver on the truck**


Its worth noting that we position ourselves as a second driver on a truck that helps the truck drive more miles each day. **** Trucks powered by Javelin will operate fully autonomously when driven by Javelin (Level 4), but not operate autonomously in every and all possible condition, they don’t need to.


> Keeping the human driver in the truck is a power play that unlocks flexibility


While offering this form of automation is unique, its an operational modality our partners are deeply familiar with. Several fleets use a pair of drivers today, commonly referred to as team-drivers, to make trucks drive longer.


With addition of just a few driving hours per day, this approach has the potential to increase trucking capacity, alleviate challenges of labor shortages, increase driver earnings, comfort and safety while on the road. *Imagine being able to Facetime your kids while the truck chugs along.* It also gives us the opportunity to build an asset-light, high margin businesses, without needing to solve the extremely challenging problem of end-to-end driverless as the first step.


### **Still not an easy task**


Of course, this is still not an easy task. We are all well aware of the long tail problem in autonomy. Risk, exposure and uncertainty hinges on variables like location, timing, weather, traffic and others. Some of it predictable, some of it not. To address these challenges, finding a subset of conditions that are conducive to automated driving is crucial and so is planning for it from the get go.


> In the Robo-taxi world, companies focus on driving in good weather, avoiding unprotected left turns, choosing longer routes, and avoiding specific streets with high variability or risk, to get to market faster.


In the Robo-trucking world, one solution is to have a driver onboard the vehicle and launch in environments where variables are few and predictable, allowing for more control over risks and uncertainties of the journey. Just keep the unit economics in check!
